source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'The So-called Babylonian Job', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Shubshi-meshre-Shakkan, named in the poem, loses everything while guiltless — office, friends, health, even his own god's face — the opening hymn still praising Marduk: I will praise the lord of wisdom. The Babylonian Job begins.
summary.zh: 詩中點名的主人蘇布希-美什烈-沙坎無辜失去一切——官職、友朋、健康、乃至其神之面——開篇仍頌馬爾杜克：我將讚美智慧之主。巴比倫的約伯記由此展開。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: I will praise the lord of wisdom, the god of reason: to him the father's light, to him who walks beside a man in his trouble and saves his life from the pit — the hymn opens in praise before the suffering begins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul bel nemeqi, Tablet I (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Shubshi-meshre-Shakkan, the sufferer named in the poem, is stripped while guiltless: his office taken, his friends fled, his body a hospital of diseases, his god turned away — and no sin known to him explains any of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablet I; not verbatim.

variants.name: A man and his god
variants.summary: The Sumerian prototype of the righteous sufferer.

primary_sources.citation: Tablet I, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912), 'The So-called Babylonian Job'

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'The So-called Babylonian Job', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: My god has forsaken me and disappeared; my goddess has failed me — the sufferer's night of abandonment: dreams that bring no answer, the wife who weeps at a distance, the friends who cross the street. How long, O my lady, how long?
summary.zh: 「我神已棄我而去；我女神亦不顧我」——受苦者遭棄之夜：夢中無答，妻子隔院垂淚，故友繞道而行。「我的女主啊，還要多久，還要多久？」

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: My god has forsaken me and disappeared; my goddess has failed me and keeps at a distance — the abandonment litany: the dream that brings no answer, the wife who weeps in another room, the friend who crosses the street.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablet II (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: How long, O my lady, will your fury be unchecked? The question is asked without accusation — the sufferer assumes there is a fault, he only cannot find it — the theology of hidden guilt that the poem will overturn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablet II; not verbatim.

functions: Litany of abandonment in the theodicy genre
Theology of hidden guilt and curable sin

variants.name: The Babylonian Theodicy
variants.summary: The acrostic dialogue that answers Ludlul skeptically.

primary_sources.citation: Tablet II, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria

title.zh: 馬爾杜克遣驅邪師：復位

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'The So-called Babylonian Job', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: In dreams the answer comes: Marduk sends the exorcist who draws out the sickness, the smith who renews the body — and the sufferer is restored, office and household and praise. The lord of wisdom is praised: he turned my captivity.
summary.zh: 夢中得答：馬爾杜克遣驅邪師拔除病根、遣工匠重造軀體——受苦者官職、家室、讚譽盡復。智慧之主受頌讚：「他使我的被擄者歸回。」

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In dreams the answer comes: a young exorcist with a signet draws out the sickness root and branch; a smith restores the body as a smith restores a broken vessel — the dream-rite of Marduk's mercy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablets III-IV (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The restoration follows in fact: office, household and health return, and the closing hymn praises the lord of wisdom who turned the sufferer's captivity — the Babylonian Job ends in praise as it began.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ludlul, Tablets III-IV; not verbatim.

functions: Arc of the theodicy liturgy: praise-abandonment-restoration-praise

primary_sources.citation: Tablets III-IV, trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria

region.zh: 巴比倫淨化神殿（伊拉克）

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'A Prayer to Every God', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: Has he vexed a god, despised a goddess, offended a father, slighted a mother? The penitent does not know his sin, so the prayer names every possibility to every god — the liturgy of the unknown transgression.
summary.zh: 「他是否觸怒男神？輕慢女神？冒犯父親？輕忽母親？」懺悔者不知己罪，遂向諸神一一歷數諸般可能——無知之罪的禱告儀式。

sensitivity.note: Ancient penitential text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Has he vexed a god, despised a goddess? Has he offended a father, slighted a mother? — the prayer names every possible sin because the penitent does not know his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Prayer to Every God (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: My god, my sins are seven times seven: forgive my unknown transgression, loose my fetters — the liturgy of the unknown sin, prayed to every god at once, that none be left unappeased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Prayer to Every God (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

functions: Formulaic penitence of the purification rite

variants.name: Shurpu series
variants.summary: The catalogue companion of the same rite.

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria
secondary_sources.citation: Morris Jastrow Jr., Boston, 1898, penitential psalms

region.zh: 烏魯克與尼尼微（伊拉克）

texts.period: Old Babylonian hymn, c. 1800 BCE (Wilson/Muss-Arnolt translation 1901)

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'Hymn to Ishtar', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The hymn hails the goddess in her double nature — the terror of battle whose heart is storm, the beauty whose grace fills the temples — she who turns men to women and women to men, whom kings and priests alike court.
summary.zh: 頌詩讚美女神的雙重本質——戰陣之怖，其心如暴風；聖殿之美，其恩寵盈殿——她能令男變女、女變男，君王與祭司皆傾慕之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The hymn hails Ishtar in her double nature: the terror of battle whose heart is storm, and the beauty whose grace fills the temples — she who turns a man to a woman and a woman to a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hymn to Ishtar (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kings and priests alike court her favor: she gives the throne and takes it, she leads the host and blesses the bed — the goddess of sovereignty and desire in one liturgy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hymn to Ishtar (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.

functions: Liturgical hymn of the goddess's double nature
Theology of sovereignty as the goddess's gift

variants.name: Inana's Descent
variants.summary: The narrative twin of the goddess's power.

primary_sources.citation: in Wilson, Babylonian and Assyrian Literature (1901)

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria
secondary_sources.citation: Morris Jastrow Jr., Boston, 1898, on Ishtar

source.work: Babylonian and Assyrian Literature, 'An Accadian Penitential Psalm', trans. Muss-Arnolt (1901)

summary.en: The oldest bilingual psalm of contrition: the suppliant in the dark temple, his sin unknown, his tears his offering — O my god, my transgressions are great, my sins are seven times seven — the voice of Mesopotamian penitence.
summary.zh: 最古老的雙語懺悔詩篇：懺悔者立於幽暗神殿，己罪不明，以淚為祭——「吾神啊，吾過甚重，吾罪七倍於七」——美索不達米亞懺悔之聲。

sensitivity.note: Ancient penitential text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The suppliant in the dark temple has no offering but tears: O my god, my transgressions are great, my sins are seven times seven — the bilingual psalm of contrition, Sumerian and Akkadian together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Accadian Penitential Psalm (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The psalm's turn is hope: the god who punishes can spare — the merciful turning of the terrible god sought in the oldest prayer formulas of the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Accadian Penitential Psalm (Muss-Arnolt 1901); not verbatim.

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria
secondary_sources.citation: Morris Jastrow Jr., Boston, 1898, penitential psalms

title.en: Ereshkigal, Queen of the Great Below
title.zh: 埃列什基伽勒：冥土之后

region.en: Ganzir, palace of the dead (symbolic pin at Kutha)
region.zh: 干基爾亡者宮殿（象徵性定位於庫薩）

source.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria, the house of the dead, Morris Jastrow (1898)

summary.en: The queen of the great earth is praised and petitioned: she who was dragged down as a bride and never came up — her house described, its rivers of the dead, its walls of the sunless — the underworld given its liturgy.
summary.zh: 冥土之后受頌受祈：她曾被拽入冥界為新娘、自此不得復出——其宮殿、亡者之河、無日之牆皆入頌詩——冥界由此擁有自己的祭儀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient liturgical text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ereshkigal, the queen of the great earth, was dragged down as a bride and never came up; her house is described — the rivers of the dead, the walls without sun — and her power praised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the underworld liturgical texts (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.

passages.text: The petition asks the queen for mercy for the dead of the household — the underworld given its own liturgy, the land below addressed as a kingdom with its own court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the underworld liturgical texts (Jastrow 1898); not verbatim.

variants.name: Nergal and Ereshkigal
variants.summary: The marriage myth of the underworld court.

source.work: Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament, 'Hymns to Tammuz', trans. Robert W. Rogers (1912)

summary.en: The dying shepherd is hymned in the orchard's language: the sap gone down, the green branch cut, the wailing women at the watercourse — the liturgy of the Tammuz month's mourning.
summary.zh: 垂死的牧神以果園之語受頌：汁液下沉、青枝遭斫、水渠旁哭喪的婦女——塔穆茲月哀悼祭儀之詩。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cult hymns; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The dying shepherd is hymned in the orchard's language: the sap gone down, the green branch cut, the wailing women at the watercourse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hymns to Tammuz (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lament's liturgy is fixed: the month of wailing for the husband below, and the rejoicing at his rise — the dying god's calendar in song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hymns to Tammuz (Rogers 1912); not verbatim.

functions: Liturgy of the Tammuz mourning month
Orchard imagery of the dying god

variants.name: Dumuzid's dream (Sumerian)
variants.summary: The narrative source of the liturgy.

secondary_sources.work: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria
